title: Most systems begin with a conversation
body: A client asks for something and a server responds. Your browser is a client; the computer serving a website is the server.
visual:
Client  →  Request  →  Server
Client  ←  Response ←  Server
takeaway: The client initiates; the server listens and responds.

title: Opening a page is a request flow
body: When you open ByteScroll, the browser requests the page. Vercel’s server finds the built files and returns HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
takeaway: A simple request can trigger several pieces of work behind one URL.

title: Your turn: identify the client
body: You open a weather app and it requests today’s forecast from an API. What is acting as the client?
explanation: The weather app initiates the request, so it is the client. The API receives the request and responds as the server.

wrong_feedback.b: The API is listening and responding, which is the server role.
wrong_feedback.c: The database may supply data behind the API, but it did not initiate the request.

title: Fast can mean two different things
body: Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests a system handles during a period of time.
visual:
Latency: one request → 120 ms
Throughput: 1,000 requests → one second
takeaway: Latency measures waiting; throughput measures volume.

title: A coffee shop explains performance
body: The wait for one coffee is latency. The number of coffees the shop makes per hour is throughput. Adding another barista may improve throughput without making one coffee much faster.
visual:
1 coffee / 4 min = latency
90 coffees / hour = throughput
takeaway: A system can have low latency but still run out of total capacity.

title: Your turn: name the measurement
body: A dashboard reports that the API handled 5,000 requests in one second. What is it measuring?
explanation: Requests per second measures the volume handled over time, which is throughput.

wrong_feedback.a: Latency would describe how long an individual request took.
wrong_feedback.c: Availability describes whether the system can be reached, not its request volume.

hint: Look for a quantity of work divided by time.

title: Remember expensive answers
body: A cache keeps frequently needed data in a faster location. Future requests can reuse that data instead of repeating slower database or network work.
visual:
Request → Cache hit → Fast response
        ↘ Cache miss → Database
takeaway: Caching trades some freshness and complexity for speed and reduced load.

title: Popular profiles are good cache candidates
body: If thousands of people view the same public profile, the service can cache it briefly instead of querying the database for every viewer.
visual: Viewers → Profile cache → Database on a miss
takeaway: Repeated reads with acceptable staleness are strong caching candidates.

title: Your turn: choose what to cache
body: Which data is the safest initial cache candidate?

options.label: A public article read thousands of times
A bank balance during a transfer

explanation: A popular public article is read often and usually tolerates brief staleness. The other options are sensitive to freshness or security.

wrong_feedback.b: A changing bank balance needs strong freshness guarantees during a transfer.
wrong_feedback.c: One-time passwords are sensitive, short-lived security data—not an initial caching target.

hint: Prefer repeated reads where a slightly old value would cause little harm.

title: Quick review: diagnose the slow read
body: A product page changes once per day, receives heavy traffic, and repeatedly reads the same database row. What should you try first?

options.label: Create a new database for every request
Make the page refresh every second

explanation: This is a read-heavy, mostly stable workload. A cache can reduce repeated database work while a sensible expiry keeps the page fresh.

wrong_feedback.b: More databases do not remove the repeated identical read and add major complexity.
wrong_feedback.c: Refreshing more often increases load without addressing the bottleneck.

hint: Which tool remembers a frequently requested answer?
